question: Does oadec's model of the decoder buffer give the figures Dolby's own TrueHD encoder reports for the streams it writes?
method: Dolby Media Encoder 5.7.2's TrueHD encoder (dee_dthd_encoder) on synthetic programmes -- pink noise gated on and off against a tone, so the buffer fills ahead of the loud stretches, and white noise up to 17.4 Mbit/s, which leaves the buffer nothing to smooth -- and on an object scene written by oadec atmos-author, each encode with --extras log_format=txt, which keeps the encoder's verification report. tools/fifo_oracle.py reads the report and compares it with oadec verify --json. The encoder refuses 44.1 and 192 kHz input ('Unsupported sample-rate'), so those rates are not in the sample. The logs are not committed; the figures below are the only part of them recorded.

model.arrival: an access unit enters whole at its input_timing (Dolby 2.7), the 16-bit field unwrapped
model.output: the output_timing of the restart headers at a major sync, one frame later for every unit after it (Dolby 2.7)
model.removal: one frame after the output time: removal at the output time misses every reported depth
model.substream_depth: the bytes of the substream's segments, without its directory entry
model.decoder_depth: the segments and the directory entries of the substreams the decoder reads, and the header, major sync and extra data of every unit; a copied presentation's decoder reads the substreams of the presentation it copies (the report's rows for the 6- and 8-channel decoders of a two-channel stream)
model.allowed_substream_depth: 15 000 bytes per channel the restart header spans, as every report states it
model.data_rate: a unit's bits over the input interval to the next unit (Dolby 2.7), rounded to the bit per second like the report; the maximum is the first unit that reaches it

encodes.encode: objects from oadec atmos-author, 48 kHz, 2 s
7.1, 96 kHz, 6 s, white noise at full scale
7.1, 96 kHz, 6 s, white noise at 0.85 of full scale
7.1, 96 kHz, 6 s, white noise at 0.7 of full scale

result.calibration: removal at the output time, and the directory entry counted in a substream's own depth, were the readings the first encode refuted; every other figure fixed the reading above

corpus.where: Coco (2017) and The Incredibles (2004), whose real damage sits at their branch points: all 340 delay and 25 rate findings of Coco lie in its damage regions; none on the 55 streams without damage, the 18 branches of Up (2009) and six encoder-written deliveries included

white_noise_and_allowance.what: white noise leaves the buffer nothing to smooth, so how far the encoder fills it shows the bound it works to; each substream's peak depth against its allowance, and each decoder's against 15 000 bytes for each of its channels (2, 6, 8)

encodes.encode: 7.1, 96 kHz, 6 s, white noise at full scale
7.1, 96 kHz, 6 s, white noise at 0.85 of full scale
7.1, 96 kHz, 6 s, white noise at 0.7 of full scale

white_noise_and_allowance.reading: in every white-noise encode one substream comes nearer its allowance (90.9 to 97.6 per cent) than any decoder comes to 15 000 bytes a channel (73.5 to 93.9): the bound the encoder works to is the allowance of each substream, the one buffer.substream_depth holds a stream to

reading: The model is Dolby's: on twelve encodes -- 48 and 96 kHz, one to four substreams, objects, a rate-optimised encode, white noise up to 17.4 Mbit/s -- every figure the encoder's verifier prints comes out the same, 84 comparisons, down to the unit a peak is first reached at. The allowance of 15 000 bytes a channel is the encoder's own, stated in each report, and the one it fills to when the content lets it. Its rules warn: they describe the stream's delivery rather than its content, and on real material they fire only where the stream is already damaged.
